stem: A bank's FAQ assistant sometimes words answers creatively and occasionally drifts from the approved facts. The team wants responses to be more consistent and focused.
prompt: Which inference parameter change is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Decrease the temperature
options.why: Lower temperature makes the model favor the most likely tokens, so answers become more consistent and stay closer to the approved wording.

options.text: Increase top-p to 1.0
options.why: Raising top-p widens the pool of candidate tokens the model can sample from, which makes wording more varied, not more consistent.

options.text: Add a stop sequence after each sentence
options.why: A stop sequence only controls where generation ends. It would cut answers short without making the wording more focused or factual.

options.text: Increase the maximum output tokens
options.why: Max tokens only caps response length. Allowing longer answers gives the model more room to drift, not less.

explanation.answer: Temperature controls randomness when sampling the next token. Low values (close to 0) make outputs more deterministic and conservative, which suits factual Q&A. High values increase diversity and creativity, which suits brainstorming or creative writing.
explanation.concept: Top-p (nucleus sampling) and top-k also control randomness by limiting which candidate tokens can be sampled.
explanation.examTip: Factual/consistent → low temperature. Creative/varied → high temperature.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters

stem: A developer reads that a model supports a parameter that restricts sampling to the smallest set of candidate next tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a chosen threshold, such as 0.9.
prompt: Which parameter is this?

options.text: Max tokens
options.why: Max tokens limits response length and does not affect which tokens are candidates.

options.text: Top-p
options.why: Top-p keeps the most likely tokens until their cumulative probability reaches p, and samples only from that set.

options.text: Top-k
options.why: Top-k limits sampling to a fixed number (k) of the most likely tokens, not to a cumulative probability threshold.

options.text: Stop sequence
options.why: A stop sequence tells the model when to stop generating. It does not filter candidate tokens.

explanation.answer: Top-p (nucleus sampling) limits the candidate pool to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Lower top-p narrows choices to the most likely tokens, reducing randomness; higher top-p allows more diverse choices.
explanation.concept: Top-k limits candidates to the k most likely tokens. Temperature reshapes the probability distribution. All three tune the balance between consistency and creativity.
explanation.examTip: Cumulative probability threshold = top-p. Fixed number of candidates = top-k.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters

stem: An application asks an LLM to generate exactly one product tagline, but the model keeps continuing with extra taglines separated by a line containing "###".
prompt: Which inference parameter can make the model stop at the first "###"?

options.text: Temperature
options.why: Temperature changes randomness but does not stop generation at a specific string.

options.text: Top-k
options.why: Top-k limits candidate tokens and does not end generation at a delimiter.

options.text: Stop sequence
options.why: A stop sequence is a string that, when generated, causes the model to stop producing more tokens.

options.text: Embedding dimension
options.why: Embedding dimension relates to vector representations, not text generation.

explanation.answer: Stop sequences specify strings that signal the model to stop generating. They help control output structure and prevent unwanted continuation, which also saves output tokens.
explanation.concept: Combine stop sequences with clear instructions and max-token limits to control response length and format.
explanation.examTip: End output at a specific marker = stop sequence.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters

stem: A marketing team uses an LLM to brainstorm 30 unusual campaign slogans. The current outputs are repetitive and very similar to each other.
prompt: Which change is MOST likely to produce more diverse slogans?

options.text: Set temperature to 0
options.why: Temperature 0 makes outputs nearly deterministic, which increases repetition.

options.text: Reduce max tokens to 5
options.why: Very short limits may truncate slogans and do not increase diversity.

options.text: Add a stop sequence after the first word
options.why: Stopping after one word would truncate every slogan.

options.text: Increase the temperature (and possibly top-p)
options.why: Higher temperature and top-p allow less likely tokens to be chosen, increasing variety and creativity.

explanation.answer: Increasing temperature (and top-p) makes the model sample from a wider range of tokens, producing more varied and creative outputs, which suits brainstorming.
explanation.concept: Higher randomness can also increase off-topic or lower-quality outputs, so creative use cases often pair higher temperature with human selection.
explanation.examTip: Need more variety → raise temperature.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters

stem: A company wants its LLM assistant to answer questions using the latest internal policy documents. Before generating each answer, the system searches the documents for relevant passages and adds them to the prompt.
prompt: What is this technique called?

options.text: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
options.why: RAG retrieves relevant information from an external knowledge source and augments the prompt with it, so the model generates grounded answers.

options.text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
options.why: RLHF is a training method that aligns models with human preferences. It does not retrieve documents per question.

options.text: Model distillation
options.why: Distillation trains a smaller model from a larger one and does not involve retrieving documents.

options.text: Fine-tuning
options.why: Fine-tuning changes model weights through training. This system adds documents at query time without training.

explanation.answer: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves relevant content from a knowledge source (such as a vector database) at query time and supplies it to the model as context. The model then generates an answer grounded in that content.
explanation.concept: RAG keeps answers current (update documents, not the model), reduces hallucinations, can cite sources, and avoids the cost of retraining.
explanation.examTip: Retrieve relevant docs + add to prompt + generate = RAG.

references.title: What is RAG?

stem: A company wants a fully managed way to connect documents stored in Amazon S3 to a foundation model for question answering. It wants AWS to handle chunking, generating embeddings, storing vectors and retrieving relevant passages.
prompt: Which AWS capability should the company use?

options.text: Amazon Kendra
options.why: Kendra is an intelligent search service that can act as a retriever, but on its own it does not connect results to a foundation model and manage the whole RAG workflow as described.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
options.why: Bedrock Knowledge Bases is managed RAG: it ingests documents from S3, chunks them, creates embeddings, stores vectors and retrieves passages for the FM.

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
options.why: OpenSearch Serverless can store and search vectors, but the company would still have to build chunking, embedding and the connection to the model itself.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents
options.why: Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks and tool calls. An agent can use a knowledge base, but it is not the managed ingestion and retrieval pipeline being asked for.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is a fully managed RAG capability. It connects to data sources (such as Amazon S3, web crawlers, SharePoint and others), chunks and embeds content, stores vectors in a supported vector store, and retrieves relevant results, optionally generating answers with citations.
explanation.concept: Supported vector stores include Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon Neptune Analytics, Amazon S3 Vectors and third-party options.
explanation.examTip: Managed RAG on AWS = Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

references.title: Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
How Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases work

stem: A compliance team requires that every answer from an internal assistant show which source documents it was based on, so reviewers can verify accuracy.
prompt: Which design BEST supports this requirement?

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the source documents
options.why: Fine-tuning blends the documents into the model's weights, so the model cannot point to which document a given answer came from.

options.text: Lower the temperature so answers stay close to sources
options.why: Lower temperature makes answers more consistent, but it does not attach or display any source documents for reviewers.

options.text: Use RAG and return citations to the retrieved passages
options.why: RAG retrieves specific passages for each answer, so the application can show them as citations that reviewers can check.

options.text: Enable a contextual grounding check in Bedrock Guardrails
options.why: A grounding check blocks answers that are not supported by the context, but it does not show reviewers which documents were used.

explanation.answer: Because RAG grounds answers in retrieved documents, it can return the source passages as citations. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases' RetrieveAndGenerate API returns citations that link the response to source chunks.
explanation.concept: Source citation supports transparency, trust and auditing, and is part of responsible and secure AI practices in the exam guide.
explanation.examTip: Need answers with sources → RAG with citations.

references.title: Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

stem: A product catalog with prices and stock levels changes many times per day. A team wants an assistant that answers customer questions using current catalog information.
prompt: Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Pre-train a new model each week on the catalog
options.why: Pre-training is extremely expensive and would still be out of date between runs.

options.text: Rely on what the base model learned in training
options.why: The base model knows nothing about the company's current catalog.

options.text: Fine-tune the model every day on the latest catalog
options.why: Daily fine-tuning is costly and still lags behind changes that occur many times a day.

options.text: Retrieve current catalog data at query time (RAG or tools)
options.why: Retrieving data at query time always reflects the latest information without retraining the model.

explanation.answer: For frequently changing information, retrieve data at query time through RAG (documents) or tool calls (live APIs and databases). This keeps answers current and avoids retraining.
explanation.concept: Fine-tuning is better for teaching style, format or domain behavior, not for frequently changing facts.
explanation.examTip: Facts change often → retrieve at query time (RAG/tools), don't fine-tune.

references.title: What is RAG?

stem: A team is writing selection criteria for choosing a foundation model for a customer-facing chat application.
prompt: Which factors are valid FM selection criteria? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Supported languages and modalities
options.why: The model must support the languages and input types the application needs.

options.text: Latency and response speed
options.why: Customer-facing chat needs responsive answers, so latency matters.

options.text: The number of GPUs in the provider's training cluster
options.why: How a provider trained the model is not something you can evaluate or use. Selection is based on the model's observable cost, speed, quality and capabilities.

options.text: Cost per input and output token
options.why: Cost directly affects the economics of the application at scale.

options.text: The embedding dimension used by the team's knowledge base
options.why: Embedding dimension is a setting of the retrieval system, chosen separately. It does not determine which chat model to select.

explanation.answer: FM selection criteria include cost, modality, latency, multilingual support, model size and complexity, customization options, input and output length (context window), prompt caching support, accuracy on your task, and compliance constraints.
explanation.concept: Shortlist models by hard requirements (modality, languages, compliance), then compare quality, cost and latency on your own evaluation data.
explanation.examTip: Cost, modality, latency, languages, size, customization, context length, caching.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources
What is Amazon Bedrock?

stem: An application needs complex multi-step reasoning over legal contracts. Testing shows that small models miss subtle clauses while larger models catch them reliably.
prompt: Which selection decision is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Choose the larger model and accept its higher cost and latency
options.why: When smaller models fail the quality bar on complex reasoning, the extra cost of a more capable model is justified.

options.text: Choose a smaller model and lower its temperature
options.why: Lower temperature makes outputs more consistent, but it does not give a small model the reasoning ability to catch subtle clauses.

options.text: Choose a smaller model and raise its maximum output tokens
options.why: Allowing longer outputs does not improve reasoning quality. The small model would still miss subtle clauses.

options.text: Choose the smallest model and accept some missed clauses
options.why: Missed clauses in contract review create legal risk that outweighs the cost savings.

explanation.answer: Model size and complexity trade off against cost and latency. Complex reasoning tasks often require larger models; simpler tasks can use smaller ones. Base the decision on evaluation against your requirements.
explanation.concept: A hybrid approach routes simple requests to small models and complex ones to large models to balance cost and quality.
explanation.examTip: Task too complex for small models → pay for capability.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: An engineer describes the runtime steps of a RAG application when a user asks a question.
prompt: Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Retrieve chunks, embed the question, generate the answer, add the chunks
options.why: Chunks cannot be retrieved before the question is embedded, and adding them after generation means the model never uses them.

options.text: Embed the question, retrieve similar chunks, add them to the prompt, generate
options.why: This is the RAG query flow: retrieve relevant context by similarity, augment the prompt with it, then generate the answer.

options.text: Embed the question, generate a draft, retrieve chunks, then correct the draft
options.why: Generating before retrieval means the first answer is not grounded. Standard RAG retrieves first so the model answers from the context.

options.text: Generate the answer, embed it, then retrieve chunks to cite as sources
options.why: Retrieving after generation can find supporting passages, but the answer itself was not grounded in them, so it can still be wrong.

explanation.answer: At query time, RAG converts the question into an embedding, retrieves the most similar document chunks from a vector store, augments the prompt with those chunks, and asks the FM to generate an answer grounded in them.
explanation.concept: Ingestion happens earlier: documents are chunked, embedded and indexed. Retrieval quality depends on chunking, embeddings and search configuration.
explanation.examTip: Embed → retrieve → augment → generate.

references.title: How Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases work

stem: A company is identifying business applications for retrieval augmented generation.
prompt: Which application is the BEST fit for RAG?

options.text: A model that forecasts next quarter's sales from history
options.why: Sales forecasting uses numeric time-series data. It does not involve retrieving documents to answer questions.

options.text: A tool that generates marketing images from text prompts
options.why: Image generation creates new content from a prompt. It does not need to retrieve facts from a document collection.

options.text: An assistant that answers HR questions from internal handbooks
options.why: Answering from a specific body of internal documents is the core RAG use case: retrieve the relevant passages, then generate the answer.

options.text: A classifier that flags fraudulent card transactions
options.why: Fraud detection is a classification task on transaction data, usually best served by a traditional ML model.

explanation.answer: RAG fits applications that must answer from a specific, often private or frequently updated, body of knowledge: internal help desks, customer support over product documentation, policy and compliance Q&A, research assistants and sales enablement.
explanation.concept: RAG combines search with generation, so answers are both relevant to company content and naturally phrased.
explanation.examTip: Answers must come from your documents → RAG.

references.title: What is RAG?

stem: A team's application sends a long, identical system prompt and reference document with every request. They are comparing two similarly priced models; only one supports prompt caching in Amazon Bedrock.
prompt: Why should prompt caching support influence the selection?

options.text: The model learns the prompt so it no longer needs to be sent
options.why: Prompt caching does not train the model. The prompt is still sent; the processed prefix is reused for a limited time.

options.text: It expands the context window for long reference documents
options.why: Caching does not change the context window. The model's maximum input length stays the same.

options.text: Identical questions are answered from stored responses
options.why: That describes response caching in an application. Prompt caching reuses the processed prompt prefix; the model still generates a new response.

options.text: It cuts cost and latency when a long prompt prefix is reused
options.why: Cached prefix tokens are billed at a reduced rate and processed faster, which suits sending the same long system prompt and document every time.

explanation.answer: Prompt caching stores the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix for a period, so subsequent requests that share the prefix are cheaper and faster. For workloads with long, repeated context, support for prompt caching is an important selection criterion.
explanation.concept: Structure prompts with static content (instructions, documents) first and variable content (the user's question) last to maximize cache hits.
explanation.examTip: Repeated long prefix → prefer a model with prompt caching.

references.title: Prompt caching for faster model inference

stem: Users complain that an assistant's answers often end mid-sentence. Logs show responses stop exactly at 100 tokens.
prompt: What is the MOST likely cause and fix?

options.text: The max tokens limit is too low; raise it or ask for shorter answers
options.why: Responses stopping at exactly the same token count mean the max tokens setting is truncating them.

options.text: A stop sequence is triggering early; remove the stop sequences
options.why: A stop sequence ends output at a specific string, so cut-offs would vary in length. Stopping at exactly 100 tokens every time points to the length limit.

options.text: The context window is full; shorten the input prompt
options.why: A full context window causes errors or truncated input, not output that consistently stops at exactly 100 tokens.

options.text: The temperature is too low; increase it for longer answers
options.why: Temperature affects how random the wording is, not how long responses can be.

explanation.answer: The max tokens (maximum output length) parameter caps the number of generated tokens. If it is too low, responses are cut off. Increase it, or instruct the model to answer concisely so complete answers fit within the limit.
explanation.concept: Input and output length limits are both FM selection and configuration considerations; longer limits mean higher potential cost.
explanation.examTip: Answers cut off at the same length → max tokens too low.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters

stem: A RAG assistant often answers with information from the wrong section of long manuals. Investigation shows each chunk is an entire 30-page chapter, and retrieved chunks contain many unrelated topics.
prompt: Which change is MOST likely to improve answer relevance?

options.text: Retrieve more chunks for each query
options.why: Retrieving more chapter-sized chunks adds even more unrelated text to the prompt, which makes the problem worse.

options.text: Split documents into smaller, focused chunks
options.why: Smaller, coherent chunks (or semantic or hierarchical chunking) make similarity search precise, so retrieved passages match the question.

options.text: Use an embedding model with more dimensions
options.why: A better embedding model cannot fix chunks that each mix many topics; every chunk's vector still blends unrelated content.

options.text: Lower the temperature so answers stick to the context
options.why: Temperature affects generation, not which passages are retrieved. The wrong chapters would still be in the prompt.

explanation.answer: Chunking strategy strongly affects RAG quality. Very large chunks mix many topics, weakening similarity matching and filling the context with noise. Smaller or semantically coherent chunks, or hierarchical chunking (search small chunks, return their parent context), improve precision.
explanation.concept: Other retrieval improvements include metadata filtering, hybrid search, reranking and query reformulation.
explanation.examTip: Wrong passages retrieved → revisit chunking (size, strategy).

references.title: How content chunking works for knowledge bases

stem: A team must select a model to describe product images in English, French and German.
prompt: Which two selection criteria are MOST decisive?

options.text: Embedding dimension and chunk size
options.why: These are retrieval settings, not generation model requirements.

options.text: Context window and output length
options.why: The task is describing images in three languages; input and output length are not the deciding factors.

options.text: Modality and multilingual support
options.why: The model must accept images and produce good descriptions in all three languages.

options.text: Training cutoff date and model size
options.why: Cutoff and size matter for knowledge and cost, but a model must first accept images and handle all three languages.

explanation.answer: Modality and multilingual capability are hard requirements here: without image input or support for the needed languages, a model cannot do the task regardless of its other strengths.
explanation.concept: Apply hard filters first (modality, language, compliance), then compare quality, cost and latency.
explanation.examTip: Images + several languages → filter by modality and language support.

references.title: What is Amazon Nova?

stem: A company runs two applications on the same model: a contract-clause extractor that must produce the same structured output for the same input, and a story generator for children's books.
prompt: Which settings are MOST appropriate?

options.text: High temperature for both applications
options.why: High randomness would make the extractor's structured output inconsistent from run to run.

options.text: High for the extractor and low for the story generator
options.why: This is reversed: extraction needs low randomness, and creative writing benefits from higher randomness.

options.text: Temperature 0 for both applications
options.why: Near-zero temperature would make the children's stories repetitive and predictable.

options.text: Low for the extractor and higher for the story generator
options.why: Extraction needs consistent output, so low randomness; storytelling benefits from variety, so higher randomness.

explanation.answer: Inference parameters should match the use case. Deterministic tasks such as extraction, classification and factual Q&A use low temperature/top-p; creative tasks such as stories and brainstorming use higher values.
explanation.concept: Parameters are set per request, so one model can serve both styles of application.
explanation.examTip: Structured/factual → low temperature. Creative → higher temperature.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters

stem: A global company's knowledge base contains HR policies for 20 countries. Employees in Germany sometimes receive answers based on US policies.
prompt: Which RAG improvement BEST addresses this?

options.text: Tag documents by country and filter retrieval on the user's country
options.why: Metadata filtering restricts retrieval to the policies that apply to the user, so German employees get German policies.

options.text: Lower the temperature so answers follow the documents closely
options.why: The model is already following documents; they are just the wrong country's. Temperature does not change which documents are retrieved.

options.text: Add a reranker to reorder the retrieved passages
options.why: A reranker scores relevance to the question, but US and German policies on the same topic are equally relevant. It cannot know the user's country.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the German HR policies
options.why: Fine-tuning does not control retrieval, would need repeating for every country, and would not stop US documents from being retrieved.

explanation.answer: Metadata filtering narrows retrieval to documents whose attributes match the query context, such as country, department, product or date. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports metadata on documents and filters at query time.
explanation.concept: Retrieval precision matters as much as model quality. Filtering, chunking, hybrid search and reranking all improve RAG relevance.
explanation.examTip: Right documents for the right user → metadata filtering.

references.title: How Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases work

stem: Business users want to ask questions such as "What were total sales by region last quarter?" in natural language, and the answer must be computed from tables in a data warehouse, not from documents.
prompt: Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Embed each table row and use vector search to find the totals
options.why: Vector search finds similar text. It cannot reliably add up values across many rows to compute totals.

options.text: Generate SQL from the question and run it against the warehouse
options.why: Text-to-SQL (for example structured data retrieval in Bedrock Knowledge Bases) computes accurate totals from the tables and grounds the answer in them.

options.text: Export the tables to text files and add them to a knowledge base
options.why: Document retrieval returns passages, not computed aggregates, so the model would have to guess the totals.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on last quarter's sales report
options.why: A fine-tuned model cannot query current data and would not compute accurate totals for new questions.

explanation.answer: For structured data, RAG uses query generation rather than vector similarity: the FM translates the question into SQL, the query runs against the data store, and the results ground the answer. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports structured data retrieval from sources such as Amazon Redshift.
explanation.concept: Choose retrieval by data type: unstructured text → vector search; structured tables → text-to-SQL; relationships → graph-based retrieval.
explanation.examTip: Numbers from tables → generate and run SQL, not vector search.

references.title: Retrieve data and generate AI responses with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

stem: A healthcare startup expects it will need to adapt a model's tone and terminology with its own examples later, and it wants to stay within Amazon Bedrock.
prompt: Which selection criterion does this introduce?

options.text: Context window: the maximum input length the model accepts
options.why: Context length matters for long inputs, but the requirement here is adapting the model's tone and terminology with examples.

options.text: Modality: whether the model accepts images as input
options.why: Modality is a valid criterion, but nothing in the scenario involves images.

options.text: Customization: whether the model supports fine-tuning in Bedrock
options.why: Only some models support fine-tuning in Amazon Bedrock, so planning to adapt tone with examples makes this the deciding criterion.

options.text: Latency: how quickly the model starts responding
options.why: Latency is a valid criterion, but the scenario's stated need is future customization.

explanation.answer: Customization is an FM selection criterion: some models in Amazon Bedrock support fine-tuning, continued pre-training or distillation, while others can only be used as-is with prompts and RAG.
explanation.concept: Prefer prompt engineering and RAG first; plan for customization only if they are insufficient.
explanation.examTip: Need to adapt the model later → pick one that supports customization.

references.title: Customize your model (Amazon Bedrock)

stem: An architect lists the components needed for a document-based RAG application.
prompt: Which components are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A GPU cluster to pre-train a new foundation model
options.why: RAG uses existing models. Pre-training is not required.

options.text: A vector store to index and search the embeddings
options.why: A vector store holds embeddings and performs similarity search at query time.

options.text: A diffusion model
options.why: Diffusion models generate images and are not part of text RAG.

options.text: A reinforcement learning reward function
options.why: RAG does not involve reinforcement learning.

options.text: An embedding model to convert chunks and queries into vectors
options.why: Embeddings enable semantic retrieval of relevant chunks.

explanation.answer: A document RAG application needs a data source, a chunking step, an embedding model, a vector store for similarity search, and a generation model (LLM) to write answers from retrieved context.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases assembles these components for you, including managed ingestion and vector store integration.
explanation.examTip: RAG = data + chunking + embedding model + vector store + LLM.

references.title: How Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases work

stem: A team must pick between two models for a live chat feature. Model X has slightly better quality but takes much longer to start responding. Model Y is slightly weaker but responds quickly. User research shows that waiting more than two seconds causes many users to abandon the chat.
prompt: Which model should the team MOST likely choose, assuming Model Y meets the quality bar?

options.text: Model X, because higher quality outweighs a slower start
options.why: Model Y already meets the quality bar, and research shows the slow start makes users abandon the chat.

options.text: Model X with response streaming enabled
options.why: Streaming shows tokens as they are generated, but Model X is slow to produce its first token, which is the delay users notice.

options.text: Model X with a lower maximum output token limit
options.why: Capping output length shortens long answers but does not make the first token arrive sooner.

options.text: Model Y, because it meets the quality bar and responds quickly
options.why: When both models meet quality needs, the faster one better serves an interactive feature where delays cause abandonment.

explanation.answer: Latency is a key FM selection criterion for interactive applications. If a faster model meets the quality bar, it usually delivers better user experience and lower cost.
explanation.concept: Streaming responses and shorter prompts also reduce perceived latency.
explanation.examTip: Interactive + meets quality → choose the faster model.

references.title: Generative AI Lens: AWS Well-Architected

stem: A RAG assistant sometimes adds information that is not in the retrieved documents. The team wants it to answer only from the provided context and say when the answer is not available.
prompt: Which change BEST supports this?

options.text: Limit answers to the given context; add a grounding check
options.why: Explicit grounding instructions plus an automated grounding check reduce answers that go beyond the retrieved sources.

options.text: Retrieve more chunks per query so every answer is covered
options.why: More context can help coverage, but it does not stop the model from adding facts that are not in the documents.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the same documents as the knowledge base
options.why: Fine-tuning adds knowledge to the weights but does not make the model refuse when the answer is missing from the retrieved context.

options.text: Set the temperature to zero so answers are deterministic
options.why: Deterministic output can still contain unsupported claims. Temperature does not enforce grounding.

explanation.answer: Grounding techniques keep RAG answers faithful to sources: clear instructions to use only the provided context, permission to say the answer is unknown, citation requirements, and automated checks such as Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding, which flags responses not supported by the source or not relevant to the query.
explanation.concept: Hallucination detection and grounding methods also appear in Domain 5 (security and governance).
explanation.examTip: Answers go beyond sources → grounding instructions + contextual grounding check.

references.title: Contextual grounding check (Amazon Bedrock Guardrails)

stem: A developer sets top-k to 1 for a text-generation request.
prompt: What is the expected effect?

options.text: The model generates a single token and then stops
options.why: Top-k limits the candidates at each step, not the total length of the response.

options.text: The model always picks the most likely next token
options.why: With k = 1 only the top-ranked token is considered at each step (greedy decoding), so the output is highly deterministic.

options.text: The model samples from the top 1% most likely tokens
options.why: That resembles top-p, which uses a cumulative probability. Top-k uses a fixed number of candidate tokens.

options.text: The model returns only the top-ranked retrieved passage
options.why: Retrieval has its own result-count setting. Top-k in inference parameters controls token sampling.

explanation.answer: Top-k restricts sampling to the k most likely next tokens. With k = 1 the model always picks the most probable token (greedy decoding), producing deterministic, conservative output. Larger k allows more variety.
explanation.concept: Temperature, top-p and top-k all shape randomness; length is controlled by max tokens and stop sequences.
explanation.examTip: Top-k = number of candidate tokens. k = 1 → deterministic.

references.title: Influence response generation with inference parameters
